content.text: The Power of Vulnerability | Brené Brown | TED

locator.quote: The Power of Vulnerability | Brené Brown | TED

content.text:
[00:16.860] So, I'll start with this: a couple years ago, an event planner called me

[00:20.345] because I was going to do a speaking event.

[00:22.418] And she called, and she said,

[00:24.132] "I'm really struggling with how to write about you on the little flyer."

[00:27.728] And I thought, "Well, what's the struggle?"

[00:30.488] And she said, "Well, I saw you speak,

[00:32.416] and I'm going to call you a researcher, I think,

[00:34.925] but I'm afraid if I call you a researcher, no one will come,

[00:37.837] because they'll think you're boring and irrelevant."

[00:40.320] (Laughter)

[00:41.345] And I was like, "Okay."

[00:42.945] And she said, "But the thing I liked about your talk

[00:45.447] is you're a storyteller.

[00:46.687] So I think what I'll do is just call you a storyteller."

[00:49.990] And of course, the academic, insecure part of me

[00:52.990] was like, "You're going to call me a what?"

[00:55.324] And she said, "I'm going to call you a storyteller."

[00:57.896] And I was like, "Why not 'magic pixie'?"

[01:00.769] (Laughter)

[01:03.648] I was like, "Let me think about this for a second."

[01:07.291] I tried to call deep on my courage.

[01:09.854] And I thought, you know, I am a storyteller.

[01:12.990] I'm a qualitative researcher.

[01:14.418] I collect stories; that's what I do.

[01:16.656] And maybe stories are just data with a soul.

[01:19.585] And maybe I'm just a storyteller.

[01:21.990] And so I said, "You know what?

[01:23.673] Why don't you just say I'm a researcher-storyteller."

[01:26.338] And she went, "Ha ha. There's no such thing."

[01:29.990] (Laughter)

[01:31.697] So I'm a researcher-storyteller, and I'm going to talk to you today --

[01:35.698] we're talking about expanding perception --

[01:37.771] and so I want to talk to you and tell some stories

[01:40.177] about a piece of my research that fundamentally expanded my perception

[01:45.360] and really actually changed the way that I live and love

[01:48.273] and work and parent.

[01:50.093] And this is where my story starts.

[01:52.990] When I was a young researcher, doctoral student,

[01:55.697] my first year, I had a research professor who said to us,

[01:59.698] "Here's the thing, if you cannot measure it, it does not exist."

[02:05.374] And I thought he was just sweet-talking me.

[02:08.339] I was like, "Really?" and he was like, "Absolutely."

[02:10.800] And so you have to understand

[02:13.077] that I have a bachelor's and a master's in social work,

[02:15.681] and I was getting my Ph.D. in social work, so my entire academic career

[02:19.079] was surrounded by people who kind of believed in the "life's messy, love it."

[02:25.474] And I'm more of the, "life's messy, clean it up, organize it

[02:30.926] and put it into a bento box."

[02:32.727] (Laughter)

[02:35.020] And so to think that I had found my way, to found a career that takes me --

[02:40.355] really, one of the big sayings in social work is,

[02:43.712] "Lean into the discomfort of the work."

[02:46.537] And I'm like, knock discomfort upside the head

[02:49.093] and move it over and get all A's.

[02:51.395] That was my mantra.

[02:54.990] So I was very excited about this.

[02:56.990] And so I thought, you know what, this is the career for me,

[02:59.990] because I am interested in some messy topics.

[03:02.990] But I want to be able to make them not messy.

[03:05.385] I want to understand them.

[03:06.731] I want to hack into these things that I know are important

[03:10.332] and lay the code out for everyone to see.

[03:12.990] So where I started was with connection.

[03:15.673] Because, by the time you're a social worker for 10 years,

[03:19.109] what you realize is that connection is why we're here.

[03:23.840] It's what gives purpose and meaning to our lives.

[03:27.076] This is what it's all about.

[03:28.886] It doesn't matter whether you talk to people

[03:31.007] who work in social justice, mental health and abuse and neglect,

[03:34.123] what we know is that connection, the ability to feel connected, is --

[03:39.948] neurobiologically that's how we're wired --

[03:41.990] it's why we're here.

[03:43.393] So I thought, you know what, I'm going to start with connection.

[03:47.067] Well, you know that situation

[03:48.988] where you get an evaluation from your boss,

[03:51.520] and she tells you 37 things that you do really awesome,

[03:54.330] and one "opportunity for growth?"

[03:56.728] (Laughter)

[03:59.196] And all you can think about is that opportunity for growth, right?

[04:02.688] Well, apparently this is the way my work went as well,

[04:05.410] because, when you ask people about love, they tell you about heartbreak.

[04:10.411] When you ask people about belonging,

[04:13.069] they'll tell you their most excruciating experiences of being excluded.

[04:17.045] And when you ask people about connection,

[04:19.570] the stories they told me were about disconnection.

[04:23.118] So very quickly -- really about six weeks into this research --

[04:26.167] I ran into this unnamed thing that absolutely unraveled connection

[04:32.213] in a way that I didn't understand or had never seen.

[04:35.109] And so I pulled back out of the research

[04:37.110] and thought, I need to figure out what this is.

[04:39.364] And it turned out to be shame.

[04:43.212] And shame is really easily understood as the fear of disconnection:

[04:47.213] Is there something about me that, if other people know it or see it,

[04:51.793] that I won't be worthy of connection?

[04:55.593] The things I can tell you about it:

[04:57.299] It's universal; we all have it.

[04:58.990] The only people who don't experience shame

[05:01.014] have no capacity for human empathy or connection.

[05:03.372] No one wants to talk about it,

[05:04.990] and the less you talk about it, the more you have it.

[05:09.005] What underpinned this shame, this "I'm not good enough," --

[05:14.195] which, we all know that feeling:

[05:15.823] "I'm not blank enough. I'm not thin enough,

[05:17.896] rich enough, beautiful enough, smart enough, promoted enough."

[05:21.174] The thing that underpinned this was excruciating vulnerability.

[05:26.862] This idea of, in order for connection to happen,

[05:30.990] we have to allow ourselves to be seen, really seen.

[05:36.061] And you know how I feel about vulnerability. I hate vulnerability.

[05:39.283] And so I thought, this is my chance to beat it back with my measuring stick.

[05:43.805] I'm going in, I'm going to figure this stuff out,

[05:46.520] I'm going to spend a year, I'm going to totally deconstruct shame,

[05:49.854] I'm going to understand how vulnerability works,

[05:52.156] and I'm going to outsmart it.

[05:54.640] So I was ready, and I was really excited.

[06:00.239] As you know, it's not going to turn out well.

[06:02.406] (Laughter)

[06:04.943] You know this.

[06:06.561] So, I could tell you a lot about shame,

[06:08.474] but I'd have to borrow everyone else's time.

[06:10.595] But here's what I can tell you that it boils down to --

[06:13.476] and this may be one of the most important things that I've ever learned

[06:16.882] in the decade of doing this research.

[06:20.068] My one year turned into six years:

[06:24.284] Thousands of stories, hundreds of long interviews, focus groups.

[06:28.990] At one point, people were sending me journal pages

[06:31.395] and sending me their stories --

[06:33.256] thousands of pieces of data in six years.

[06:37.272] And I kind of got a handle on it.

[06:38.990] I kind of understood, this is what shame is, this is how it works.

[06:43.452] I wrote a book, I published a theory, but something was not okay --

[06:49.723] and what it was is that, if I roughly took the people I interviewed

[06:53.903] and divided them into people who really have a sense of worthiness --

[07:00.499] that's what this comes down to, a sense of worthiness --

[07:03.285] they have a strong sense of love and belonging --

[07:06.531] and folks who struggle for it,

[07:08.206] and folks who are always wondering if they're good enough.

[07:11.330] There was only one variable that separated

[07:13.593] the people who have a strong sense of love and belonging

[07:16.357] and the people who really struggle for it.

[07:18.640] And that was, the people who have a strong sense of love and belonging

[07:22.382] believe they're worthy of love and belonging.

[07:25.704] That's it.

[07:27.505] They believe they're worthy.

[07:30.736] And to me, the hard part of the one thing that keeps us out of connection

[07:36.578] is our fear that we're not worthy of connection,

[07:39.817] was something that, personally and professionally,

[07:42.244] I felt like I needed to understand better.

[07:44.807] So what I did is I took all of the interviews

[07:49.808] where I saw worthiness, where I saw people living that way,

[07:52.650] and just looked at those.

[07:55.314] What do these people have in common?

[07:57.386] I have a slight office supply addiction, but that's another talk.

[08:02.053] So I had a manila folder, and I had a Sharpie,

[08:05.554] and I was like, what am I going to call this research?

[08:08.198] And the first words that came to my mind were "whole-hearted."

[08:11.807] These are whole-hearted people, living from this deep sense of worthiness.

[08:15.347] So I wrote at the top of the manila folder,

[08:18.227] and I started looking at the data.

[08:20.180] In fact, I did it first in a four-day, very intensive data analysis,

[08:26.197] where I went back, pulled the interviews, the stories, pulled the incidents.

[08:29.798] What's the theme? What's the pattern?

[08:32.370] My husband left town with the kids

[08:35.371] because I always go into this Jackson Pollock crazy thing,

[08:38.372] where I'm just writing and in my researcher mode.

[08:43.625] And so here's what I found.

[08:48.114] What they had in common was a sense of courage.

[08:51.624] And I want to separate courage and bravery for you for a minute.

[08:54.745] Courage, the original definition of courage,

[08:57.210] when it first came into the English language --

[08:59.473] it's from the Latin word "cor," meaning "heart" --

[09:01.850] and the original definition was to tell the story of who you are

[09:04.885] with your whole heart.

[09:07.059] And so these folks had, very simply, the courage to be imperfect.

[09:13.632] They had the compassion to be kind to themselves first and then to others,

[09:18.633] because, as it turns out,

[09:19.856] we can't practice compassion with other people

[09:22.114] if we can't treat ourselves kindly.

[09:24.259] And the last was they had connection, and -- this was the hard part --

[09:28.680] as a result of authenticity,

[09:31.681] they were willing to let go of who they thought they should be

[09:34.990] in order to be who they were, which you have to absolutely do that

[09:39.618] for connection.

[09:43.323] The other thing that they had in common was this:

[09:50.910] They fully embraced vulnerability.

[09:55.679] They believed that what made them vulnerable made them beautiful.

[10:06.141] They didn't talk about vulnerability being comfortable,

[10:09.990] nor did they really talk about it being excruciating --

[10:12.840] as I had heard it earlier in the shame interviewing.

[10:15.342] They just talked about it being necessary.

[10:18.633] They talked about the willingness to say, "I love you" first ...

[10:24.378] the willingness to do something where there are no guarantees ...

[10:31.283] the willingness to breathe through waiting for the doctor to call

[10:35.642] after your mammogram.

[10:38.631] They're willing to invest in a relationship

[10:41.920] that may or may not work out.

[10:44.465] They thought this was fundamental.

[10:47.442] I personally thought it was betrayal.

[10:50.847] I could not believe I had pledged allegiance to research, where our job --

[10:55.467] you know, the definition of research is to control and predict,

[10:59.555] to study phenomena for the explicit reason to control and predict.

[11:04.222] And now my mission to control and predict

[11:08.612] had turned up the answer that the way to live is with vulnerability

[11:12.205] and to stop controlling and predicting.

[11:14.327] This led to a little breakdown --

[11:16.902] (Laughter)

[11:21.990] -- which actually looked more like this.

[11:24.990] (Laughter)

[11:26.507] And it did.

[11:28.508] I call it a breakdown; my therapist calls it a spiritual awakening.

[11:31.712] (Laughter)

[11:32.970] A spiritual awakening sounds better than breakdown,

[11:35.411] but I assure you, it was a breakdown.

[11:37.212] And I had to put my data away and go find a therapist.

[11:40.140] Let me tell you something: you know who you are

[11:42.395] when you call your friends and say, "I think I need to see somebody.

[11:45.659] Do you have any recommendations?"

[11:47.489] Because about five of my friends were like,

[11:49.562] "Wooo, I wouldn't want to be your therapist."

[11:51.730] (Laughter)

[11:54.492] I was like, "What does that mean?"

[11:56.493] And they're like, "I'm just saying, you know.

[11:59.724] Don't bring your measuring stick."

[12:01.725] (Laughter)

[12:04.485] I was like, "Okay."

[12:06.545] So I found a therapist.

[12:08.403] My first meeting with her, Diana --

[12:12.109] I brought in my list of the way the whole-hearted live, and I sat down.

[12:16.427] And she said, "How are you?"

[12:18.260] And I said, "I'm great. I'm okay."

[12:21.879] She said, "What's going on?"

[12:23.427] And this is a therapist who sees therapists,

[12:26.070] because we have to go to those, because their B.S. meters are good.

[12:31.307] (Laughter)

[12:33.736] And so I said, "Here's the thing, I'm struggling."

[12:37.593] And she said, "What's the struggle?"

[12:40.442] And I said, "Well, I have a vulnerability issue.

[12:42.727] And I know that vulnerability is the core of shame and fear

[12:48.106] and our struggle for worthiness,

[12:49.727] but it appears that it's also the birthplace of joy, of creativity,

[12:55.427] of belonging, of love.

[12:57.776] And I think I have a problem, and I need some help."

[13:03.236] And I said, "But here's the thing: no family stuff, no childhood shit."

[13:08.427] (Laughter)

[13:10.427] "I just need some strategies."

[13:13.427] (Laughter)

[13:17.427] (Applause)

[13:21.036] Thank you.

[13:24.283] So she goes like this.

[13:27.427] (Laughter)

[13:29.807] And then I said, "It's bad, right?"

[13:32.427] And she said, "It's neither good nor bad."

[13:35.427] (Laughter)

[13:37.284] "It just is what it is."

[13:39.664] And I said, "Oh my God, this is going to suck."

[13:42.427] (Laughter)

[13:45.593] And it did, and it didn't.

[13:47.871] And it took about a year.

[13:49.958] And you know how there are people

[13:51.998] that, when they realize that vulnerability and tenderness are important,

[13:56.046] that they surrender and walk into it.

[13:59.231] A: that's not me,

[14:01.215] and B: I don't even hang out with people like that.

[14:03.636] (Laughter)

[14:06.427] For me, it was a yearlong street fight.

[14:09.752] It was a slugfest.

[14:11.339] Vulnerability pushed, I pushed back.

[14:13.593] I lost the fight,

[14:16.704] but probably won my life back.

[14:18.727] And so then I went back into the research

[14:20.727] and spent the next couple of years

[14:22.427] really trying to understand what they, the whole-hearted,

[14:25.427] what choices they were making, and what we are doing with vulnerability.

[14:31.427] Why do we struggle with it so much?

[14:33.791] Am I alone in struggling with vulnerability?

[14:37.190] No.

[14:38.427] So this is what I learned.

[14:41.959] We numb vulnerability --

[14:44.680] when we're waiting for the call.

[14:46.291] It was funny, I sent something out on Twitter and on Facebook

[14:49.204] that says, "How would you define vulnerability?

[14:51.502] What makes you feel vulnerable?"

[14:53.074] And within an hour and a half, I had 150 responses.

[14:55.822] Because I wanted to know what's out there.

[15:01.204] Having to ask my husband for help because I'm sick, and we're newly married;

[15:06.251] initiating sex with my husband;

[15:08.282] initiating sex with my wife;

[15:11.020] being turned down; asking someone out;

[15:14.022] waiting for the doctor to call back;

[15:16.085] getting laid off; laying off people.

[15:18.451] This is the world we live in.

[15:20.962] We live in a vulnerable world.

[15:23.954] And one of the ways we deal with it is we numb vulnerability.

[15:27.688] And I think there's evidence --

[15:29.427] and it's not the only reason this evidence exists,

[15:31.832] but I think it's a huge cause --

[15:33.965] We are the most in-debt ...

[15:38.538] obese ...

[15:40.910] addicted and medicated adult cohort in U.S. history.

[15:48.315] The problem is -- and I learned this from the research --

[15:51.609] that you cannot selectively numb emotion.

[15:55.291] You can't say, here's the bad stuff.

[15:58.427] Here's vulnerability, here's grief, here's shame,

[16:00.827] here's fear, here's disappointment.

[16:02.527] I don't want to feel these.

[16:04.427] I'm going to have a couple of beers and a banana nut muffin.

[16:07.333] (Laughter)

[16:10.043] I don't want to feel these.

[16:11.936] And I know that's knowing laughter.

[16:13.936] I hack into your lives for a living.

[16:16.427] God.

[16:18.427] (Laughter)

[16:20.998] You can't numb those hard feelings

[16:23.780] without numbing the other affects, our emotions.

[16:26.438] You cannot selectively numb.

[16:27.914] So when we numb those,

[16:30.545] we numb joy,

[16:33.092] we numb gratitude,

[16:34.427] we numb happiness.

[16:37.148] And then, we are miserable,

[16:40.295] and we are looking for purpose and meaning,

[16:42.328] and then we feel vulnerable,

[16:43.784] so then we have a couple of beers and a banana nut muffin.

[16:46.616] And it becomes this dangerous cycle.

[16:51.087] One of the things that I think we need to think about

[16:54.244] is why and how we numb.

[16:56.928] And it doesn't just have to be addiction.

[17:00.477] The other thing we do is we make everything that's uncertain certain.

[17:05.427] Religion has gone from a belief in faith and mystery to certainty.

[17:10.537] "I'm right, you're wrong. Shut up."

[17:14.187] That's it.

[17:16.611] Just certain.

[17:18.340] The more afraid we are, the more vulnerable we are,

[17:20.780] the more afraid we are.

[17:22.189] This is what politics looks like today.

[17:24.220] There's no discourse anymore.

[17:25.919] There's no conversation.

[17:27.807] There's just blame.

[17:29.055] You know how blame is described in the research?

[17:32.553] A way to discharge pain and discomfort.

[17:37.616] We perfect.

[17:38.830] If there's anyone who wants their life to look like this, it would be me,

[17:42.632] but it doesn't work.

[17:43.883] Because what we do is we take fat from our butts and put it in our cheeks.

[17:47.527] (Laughter)

[17:50.990] Which just, I hope in 100 years, people will look back and go, "Wow."

[17:54.427] (Laughter)

[17:56.974] And we perfect, most dangerously, our children.

[18:00.427] Let me tell you what we think about children.

[18:02.594] They're hardwired for struggle when they get here.

[18:05.427] And when you hold those perfect little babies in your hand,

[18:08.333] our job is not to say, "Look at her, she's perfect.

[18:11.315] My job is just to keep her perfect --

[18:13.235] make sure she makes the tennis team by fifth grade and Yale by seventh."

[18:16.666] That's not our job.

[18:17.927] Our job is to look and say,

[18:19.560] "You know what? You're imperfect, and you're wired for struggle,

[18:22.600] but you are worthy of love and belonging."

[18:25.501] That's our job.

[18:27.104] Show me a generation of kids raised like that,

[18:29.358] and we'll end the problems, I think, that we see today.

[18:31.983] We pretend that what we do doesn't have an effect on people.

[18:38.871] We do that in our personal lives.

[18:40.529] We do that corporate --

[18:41.776] whether it's a bailout, an oil spill ...

[18:45.386] a recall.

[18:46.570] We pretend like what we're doing

[18:48.571] doesn't have a huge impact on other people.

[18:51.427] I would say to companies, this is not our first rodeo, people.

[18:55.769] We just need you to be authentic and real and say ...

[18:59.919] "We're sorry. We'll fix it."

[19:05.535] But there's another way, and I'll leave you with this.

[19:08.331] This is what I have found:

[19:09.736] To let ourselves be seen, deeply seen, vulnerably seen ...

[19:16.891] to love with our whole hearts, even though there's no guarantee --

[19:21.304] and that's really hard,

[19:22.582] and I can tell you as a parent, that's excruciatingly difficult --

[19:28.495] to practice gratitude and joy in those moments of terror,

[19:32.701] when we're wondering, "Can I love you this much?

[19:35.038] Can I believe in this this passionately?

[19:37.248] Can I be this fierce about this?"

[19:39.202] just to be able to stop and, instead of catastrophizing what might happen,

[19:42.803] to say, "I'm just so grateful,

[19:44.804] because to feel this vulnerable means I'm alive."

[19:48.748] And the last, which I think is probably the most important,

[19:52.434] is to believe that we're enough.

[19:54.664] Because when we work from a place, I believe, that says, "I'm enough" ...

[20:00.743] then we stop screaming and start listening,

[20:04.735] we're kinder and gentler to the people around us,

[20:07.086] and we're kinder and gentler to ourselves.

[20:10.125] That's all I have. Thank you.

[20:11.627] (Applause)

goal_candidates.snippet: [00:16.860] So, I'll start with this: a couple years ago, an event planner called me
[00:24.132] "I'm really struggling with how to write about you on the little flyer."
[01:16.656] And maybe stories are just data with a soul.
[03:12.990] So where I started was with connection.
[03:43.393] So I thought, you know what, I'm going to start with connection.
